I Came for a Tactical Shooter. I Left a Different Person.

There are games you play to pass the time. There are games you play because you're bored. There are games you play because your friends are online.

And then there is Ready or Not.

I genuinely don't know how to put into words what this game has done to me. I installed it expecting a tactical shooter. I expected guns, missions, suspects, some good old-fashioned door kicking and perhaps the occasional questionable decision from my teammates.

I was not prepared.

I was not prepared for the silence before entering a room. I was not prepared for the sound of footsteps on the other side of a door. I was not prepared for the moment when a suspect refuses to surrender, when a teammate shouts for cover, or when everything goes horribly wrong in a fraction of a second.

But most importantly, I was not prepared for the emotional journey.

Every mission feels like it means something. Every corner feels like it could be your last. Every time I hear someone shout "POLICE, DROP YOUR WEAPON!" I feel a little part of my soul leave my body.

And yet, I keep coming back.

I have laughed. I have screamed. I have questioned my intelligence. I have stared at a loading screen wondering where my life went wrong. I have watched my carefully coordinated tactical operation collapse because one person forgot to check a corner.

But I have also experienced moments of genuine brilliance.

The feeling of clearing a building with your squad, covering each other, communicating properly and somehow making it through an entire mission without everything descending into absolute chaos is something I struggle to find in any other game.

There is something special about a game that makes you slow down. A game that makes you think before you act. A game that reminds you that sometimes the most important thing you can do is NOT pull the trigger.

And that is what makes Ready or Not so special.

It isn't simply about shooting people. It is about restraint, responsibility, teamwork and the weight of the decisions you make.

The atmosphere deserves its own appreciation. The sound design, the lighting, the environments, the voice acting, the tiny details scattered throughout every mission. Everything contributes to an experience that can be genuinely uncomfortable in the best possible way.

There are moments where I have genuinely forgotten that I am sitting at a computer playing a video game. I am no longer thinking about my keyboard or mouse. I am thinking about the room ahead, the people inside it and whether my squad is going to make it out.

And then someone on my team gets stuck in a doorway.

Immersion shattered. Humanity restored.

I also want to acknowledge the people behind this game.

To the developers, artists, sound designers, programmers, writers, animators and everyone else who contributed to this project: thank you.

I know that making a game is not easy. I know that behind every little detail that players might overlook are hours of work, problem-solving, frustration and dedication.

Most players will probably never stop to appreciate the amount of effort that goes into making a single mission feel believable. They might never think about the sound of a distant gunshot, the positioning of an object in a room or the way an environment tells a story without saying a single word.

But somebody made those decisions.

Somebody cared enough to make those details exist.

And somebody, somewhere, spent an unreasonable amount of time making sure that a door opens in a particular way.

I hope those people know that their work matters.

Because it does.

Games like this remind me why I love gaming in the first place. Not because of graphics, not because of achievements, not because of how many hours I can put into something, but because of the experiences that games can create.

The memories.

The ridiculous moments with friends.

The missions that go perfectly until the final thirty seconds.

The missions that go catastrophically wrong from the very first door.

The times when everyone is silent because something genuinely terrifying just happened.

And the occasional teammate who thinks a flashbang is a substitute for basic communication.

I don't know how many more hours I will spend playing Ready or Not. I don't know how many more missions I will complete, how many more times I will get shot through a doorway, or how many more times I will have to explain to my squad that perhaps we should try a slightly different approach.

But I do know one thing.

Years from now, when I look back at the games I played, I suspect Ready or Not will be one of the ones I remember.

Not because it was perfect.

Not because every update was flawless.

Not because every mission went according to plan.

But because it made me feel something.

And that is becoming increasingly rare.

So, to everyone at VOID Interactive: thank you for creating something that people can genuinely lose themselves in. Thank you for putting so much detail into a game that could so easily have been just another shooter. Thank you for giving us something worth talking about, laughing about, getting frustrated with and returning to.

And to whoever designed the AI that can somehow identify my exact location through three walls, a filing cabinet and what I can only assume is divine intervention:

I hope you sleep well.

You have ruined my life.

In the best possible way.

I gave this game a negative review because apparently players are expected to fix it themselves!

If, like me, you're experiencing severe LOD (Level of Detail) and texture pop-in issues, here's a potential fix:

Press  Win + R and enter:

`%LOCALAPPDATA%\ReadyOrNot\Saved\Config\Windows`

Open Engine.ini and add the following lines:

[SystemSettings]
r.ViewDistanceScale=5
r.StaticMeshLODDistanceScale=0.1
r.SkeletalMeshLODBias=-2
foliage.LODDistanceScale=3

Save the file and restart the game.

These settings increase rendering distances and force higher-detail models to remain visible at greater distances, reducing noticeable LOD transitions and object pop-in.

Be aware that this may reduce performance depending on your hardware, although I personally haven't noticed any measurable difference.

It's ridiculous that players have to resort to manually editing configuration files to fix such obvious graphical issues. This is something the developers should have addressed themselves, not left to the community to figure out.

Love this game. This is my favorite tactical shooter to play single player, and has no doubt revolutionized the tactical shooter genre in many ways, but the friendly AI needs some sorely needed updates. The amount of times I'll tell my team to do something for them to bug out and not do it is crazy. The friendly AI also seems to be part time pacifists, sometimes holding their lethal gun fire on suspects when they are being shot at, and abstaining completely from shooting noncompliant armed suspects trying to evade orders when my team have non lethal weapons like my beloved beanbag shotgun. Besides this, none of your team mates can throw a grenade into a room to save their lives, consistently throwing them right on the threshold or the side of the door where the cops are.

The enemy AI, Especially on hard, love to hold wicked angles on you and your team to where they are pretty much impossible to hit with a pump action beanbag shotgun (Especially when they are behind a window, metal bars or pipes. This is especially infuriating on valley of the dolls, where your team loves to go up and lick the windows so all of the suspects on the ground floor can see and then shoot them). I've learned to abuse the heck out of the alt button to hold my own wicked (and probably physically not accomplishable due to spines, bones and what not) angles on suspects. 

Another gripe, there's been several instances where I have dumped the entire beanbag shotgun's magazine onto armed suspects and they still refuse to surrender. I can maybe understand on maps with junkies like twisted nerve, as the subject is probably high on some illicit substance and can (At least temporarily) disregard the fact that their ribs and internals have been bean bagged to the point of being a homogenized sludge and even after being shot right in the go-nads just for  good measure. Sure, whatever. But when I'm going up against professional security or any other group, it seems pretty unlikely that they get right back up and continue to shoot at me after dumping a whole mags worth of beanbags into them. Easily some of the worst times I've had in this game is when this kind of thing occurs, no matter how many times you bean bag them, grenade them or melee them, they refuse to surrender. It ruins the whole mission and sometimes the whole run, and makes me want to play this game less. Also, is it just me or do suspects seemingly never run out of ammo? They seem to switch to their sidearms, but I've never encountered one actually stop shooting because of no ammo or any weapons they've dropped with the bolt locked back.

And yet another note, it seems to me like the pepper ball launchers are pretty much all but unusable in comparison to the beanbag shotgun. They really just don't seem like they're worth using. And as much as I love to blast suspects with the wide variety of lethal weapons, the non-lethal weapons really need some more diversity. Three nonlethal weapons (Not counting launchers, which are also pretty middling) is honestly pretty prohibitive and can get repetitive quick, especially since in commander mode (The only mode in which I and most people play), The only way to get your team to activate their perks are basically to get S ranks on missions back to back (Requiring no dead suspects).

My final but by far smallest gripe, every time you load into the department you hear a female officer say "Christ, it's really kicking off out there", In my own head canon, It's some sort of autistic fixation of hers to say those words in the exact same intonation every time Judge walks through the front doors. Some variation in voice lines for officers at the station and on your team would go a long way.

Squad AI is quite neglected, making singleplayer a rote and frustrating experience. SWAT members sometimes fail to react to being shot, cannot throw grenades properly, and demonstrate all the wrong initiative. Because squadmates don't understand how to safely take and secure a room - they do not recognize even the most obvious dangers and occupy vulnerable positions while monitoring the least dangerous angles - the player is forced to use wedges as a final recourse. And when a danger evolves into an active threat, they do not respond to that either. They usually only react to what is in view (and sometimes not even that). Thus, gameplay becomes a process of using wedges on every single door, as it is the only way you can guarantee security. Micromanagement rather than team coordination.

But even that is difficult to do safely. Sometimes squadmates do not follow orders, and when they do, it can lead to undesired behaviour. To place a wedge, the door must first be closed. The squadmate can close the door, but if there's a downed suspect or some evidence on the other side, they may choose to reopen the door to collect the evidence/restrain the suspect (possibly dying in the process, which is often followed by you or the rest of the team dying). So it is safest to close and wedge doors yourself, but again, you cannot trust your teammates to protect you in the process without specifically ordering them to do so, which - since you are often exposed from multiple angles - requires several orders for something that any human would have done automatically and without hesitation. In the time it takes to set up those orders, a threat may have appeared from any of the thresholds you are trying to secure. But all of this could have been prevented if the AI was aware of thresholds and could identify them as threats and treat them accordingly.

A big part of the issue is that most things the AI does seems to be baked into the map. Often the squadmates will delay carrying out an order because you are standing in their magical golden path when they could just walk around you while respecting your line of fire. This is sometimes fatal, as you are usually trying to provide security for them, and moving would not only endanger but often you as well. Or you may even be trying to engage suspects and they might cross your line of fire, or force you to move (destabilizing you) because you consider their task time sensitive. It isn't clear if those paths are baked or calculated, but they are too inflexible all the same. The angles that the AI hold after clearing, however, appear to be baked. Reasonable for performance and consistency. But the algorithm used to bake them isn't aware of lines of sight; It is aware of doors. The most obvious example of this is cases with windows or counters such as the lobby of the Mindjot Datacenter. The reception desk is partitioned into a separate logical room (it has a door, so this makes sense). But the reception desk "room" has a door to the kitchen. The squadmates don't know that the kitchen effectively connects to the lobby, so they don't cover it. This frequently results in suspects coming through the kitchen into the reception area, which is not covered by any teammates, leaving a nasty surprise for the player. This is compounded by the fact that two squadmates will always be standing in the corner watching the corridor door and the double doors. Those squadmates are immediately cut off from the team should a suspect move to the reception desk. This makes an otherwise safe and obvious room for double entry quite perilous, all because the squadmates can't "see" what is obviously the second most dangerous door in the room.
